newsitem.title: USA: Manpower stock up on results, encouraging European news.
newsitem.headline: Manpower stock up on results, encouraging European news.

text.p: Manpower Inc. posted stronger results Thursday and industry analysts said positive news on revenue growth in France, which accounts for a third of its business, boosted its stock by more than 18 percent.

The Milwaukee-based company reported fourth-quarter earnings of $48.1 million, or 58 cents a share, up from $36.6 million, or 45 cents a share, a year earlier. Revenues rose to $1.99 billion from $1.74 billion a year earlier.
The stock of the world's largest temporary employment company jumped $5.625, or 18.75 percent, to $35.625 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the largest percentage gainer.

Manpower Chairman Mitchell Fromstein said the company's earnings came in a bit above estimates, which also contributed to the stock's gain. "There may have been a feeling that we wouldn't make the numbers, but we came in pennies above," said Fromstein.
"There was good news on the conference call about revenue growth in France, said H. Perry Boyle of Alex. Brown, "and (Manpower) expects that strength to accelerate in 1997.
"There was nervousness about the fourth quarter, especially about the French business, which accounts for about one-third of the company's revenue base," Boyle said.

"The trend in France got stronger in January, so 1997 is off to a strong start," said William Sutherland, an analyst at Janney Montgomery Scott Inc. "That's important for the stock since it fell short of original expectations in the first half of 1996."
For the year, earnings rose to $162.3 million, or $1.95 a share, on revenues of $7.47 billion. In 1995, Manpower earned $128 million, or $1.65 a share, on revenues of $6.88 billion.
While the outlook for 1997 may appear promising, some analysts are concerned about subsidies the French government provided to French companies last year to curb unemployment.
"I'm urging caution," Boyle said. "(Manpower's) growth in France benefited from French government subsidies in 1996 that may not be there in 1997."
Sutherland, the Janney Montgomery analyst, agreed. "It's safer to assume they won't be there (in 1997)," he said.
"The tax credit is used as a motivator for employers to hire and the (French government) will probably continue them, but not at levels seen in 1996."
Jeff Silber, an analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison & Co. Inc., said Manpower officials were not too positive about prospects for continued subsidies in their comments during the conference call.
"There are no guarantees," he said. "The French government tries these things on an experimental basis."
